Triggers.value: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened

Threat.value: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
I can't rely on other people

issues.item: Triggers: Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
issues.explanation: 'Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident' is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of natural disaster. A car-crash-specific trigger suggests a different index trauma unless there is clear disaster-related context, which is not reflected elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Memory: Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage
issues.explanation: 'Rage on Recall' is not well supported by the rest of the profile, which otherwise centers on fear, vulnerability, dissociation/gaps, and interpersonal mistrust after a natural disaster. Intense rage could occur clinically, but here it lacks corroboration from threat or appraisal items and weakens overall coherence.

For a natural disaster trauma, 'related people' as a primary trigger is hard to justify unless they were directly linked to the event; with no supporting interpersonal trauma content elsewhere, this trigger is clinically questionable.

issues.item: Threat: Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
issues.explanation: The threat item about unusual silence implying imminent danger fits combat/interpersonal danger contexts more than natural disaster exposure, and it is not supported by the trigger or appraisal content here.

vignette: Leo, a second-generation American with European roots, was twenty-seven when the river broke. It was a late October flood, the water rising faster than the warning sirens could keep up. He had been walking the riverpath near his apartment, a familiar stretch of paved trail flanked by sycamores and low grass, when the current swallowed the lower bank. He watched the water cross the trail, then felt it tugging at his boots. The sky had been gray, but what stayed with him most was the sudden, absolute pressure of the water against his chest and the way the world narrowed to the sound of rushing tide and his own ragged breathing. He made it to the higher ground, but the riverpath remained locked behind a temporary fence. Over the next months, Leo found himself navigating a life that felt both familiar and fundamentally altered. As a salesperson, his days required constant movement through client sites, but the spaces he once traversed without a second thought now demanded scrutiny. He began avoiding the downtown offices where he used to close deals, finding the glass-walled lobbies and narrow corridors strangely constricting. Physical locations had become unpredictable, and he caught himself lingering in doorways, measuring distances, until he felt certain the floor would hold. Being in nature held the same familiar weight; a weekend hike or a client meeting held near the waterfront brought back the damp chill and the sense of exposure that had defined those floodwaters. What frightened him most was the quiet, emotional weight that settled over him without warning. Standing in a grocery aisle or sitting through a routine presentation, he would feel suddenly vulnerable, as though his composure were a thin layer over something raw and ready to break. His nights grew restless. Leo routinely woke during the night to check whether he was safe, pacing the bedroom, peering through the blinds, testing the locks before returning to bed. During the day, he was constantly watchful, scanning the room, noting exits, bracing for shifts he could not name. The flood did not always return as a clear picture. On occasion, he would suddenly feel or act as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, his shoulders hunching, his breath catching, before the moment passed. Some days, the memory arrived as a wave of pure emotion without image; he would feel the full emotional intensity of the event, the same terror, yet he could not place a single scene in his mind. There were parts of those hours that simply vanished, parts of the event that he simply could not remember no matter how hard he tried to piece them together. When he did manage to recall the event, however, the terror returned, bringing back the same terror he felt at the time, as if he were standing in the rising water once more. Work and routine began to carry the weight of these shifts. Leo still made his sales calls, but the habit of checking his surroundings had bled into his professional life. He stopped taking the routes that passed the riverpath, opting instead for longer, predictable drives, and he began to rely heavily on his own notes rather than asking colleagues to verify details. He had come to believe that other people simply could not be counted on to read the signs when the environment turned. His identity felt unmoored; he looked at his reflection and felt like he did not know himself anymore. The things he once found purposeful—the targets, the commissions, the weekend routines—now felt hollow, as though their lost meaning had drained away with the water. At twenty-nine, Leo now sits in a therapist’s office for the first time. He has come because the checking has become exhausting, the emotional vulnerability interrupts his client meetings, and the nights no longer rest his body. He is most afraid that the water will return without warning, but more quietly, he is hoping to understand why the world feels so fragile, and whether he can recognize himself again.
